Q: How to use StandardScaler on only specific columns in a pandas DataFrame? A:

The most common method is using these lines after "scaler = StandardScaler()":

cols_to_scale = ['power', 'time']
df[cols_to_scale] = scaler.fit_transform(df[cols_to_scale])
print(df)

Ouput:

      power      time  status
0 -1.224745 -1.224745       0
1  0.000000  0.000000       1
2  1.224745  1.224745       0

Another method is adding these lines after "df = pd.DataFrame(data)":

X = df[['power', 'time']]
y = df['status']

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(
    scaler.fit_transform(X),
    columns=X.columns,
    index=X.index
)

df_scaled = pd.concat([X_scaled, y], axis=1)
print(df_scaled)

Q: How do I code without being completely dependent on AI? A:

Honestly, I think worrying about this is probably a good sign.

The danger is not using AI. The danger is letting AI skip the part where your brain builds the model of the problem.

I’d start doing smaller projects where you force yourself to write the first version without AI. It can be ugly. It can be slow. That’s fine. Then use AI after that to compare, refactor, or explain better approaches.

DSA can help, but I wouldn’t make it the whole answer. Build things where you have to understand the moving parts: file parsers, small web apps, CLI tools, toy databases, simple ML models from scratch.

The goal is not to code like AI doesn’t exist. The goal is to stop treating AI like a substitute for understanding.

Use it as a senior engineer sitting next to you, not as your hands.

Q: Is it worth using a unique pointer for a Huffman Tree A:

A Huffman tree that uses chars for symbols (aka N=256) has a theoretical maximum depth of 255. What you're referring to is that for most cases, the deepest you'd encounter would be ~2*lg2(N), which is approximately ~16.

Q: Is it better to avoid using the mod operator when possible? A:

If len is a compile-time constant power of 2 (common in circular buffers) and i is a signed integer (the compiler can't prove it's non-negative), modulo is less efficient than a bitwise AND. This is because even if you never use negative i, C's i % len for negative i will produce a negative number that isn't simply the lower-order bits.

Here's the proof in an innocent-looking example:

#define len (1 << 10)

int f(int i) { return i % len; }

GCC actually does a quite tricky branchless idiom that requires some explanation: (https://godbolt.org/z/qze33f5d4)

        mov     edx, edi
        sar     edx, 31
        shr     edx, 22
        lea     eax, [rdi+rdx]
        and     eax, 1023
        sub     eax, edx
        ret
  1. sar (shift arithmetic right) by 31 actually fills edx with the sign-bit.
  2. shr (shift logical right) by 22 produces either 0x03FF bitmask for negative edx or 0 for positive edx.
  3. lea adds the mask to the original value.
  4. and takes the lowest 10 bits.
  5. sub subtracts the mask, ensuring the result follows C's signed modulo definition.

Now what if you make i unsigned or do the bitwise AND yourself? (https://godbolt.org/z/hbaTGGc1W)

        mov     eax, edi
        and     eax, 1023
        ret

It does simply a bitwise AND. This is unequivocally better than the previous because that had to do the same and eax, 1023.

Another option worth trying if i is incremented in a loop is to not do modulo at all and reset to 0 when you hit the modulus. This trades the extra and operation for a conditional branch that is mostly not-taken. It works for modulus not a power-of-two too.

Whether or not this makes a difference depends on if this code is in a hot-loop. I wrote some simple string-matching code for a LZ compressor, and forcing the indices to be unsigned actually made the code about 20% faster. So maybe the takeaway message is that a compiler can only optimize a modulo a power of 2 into a bitmask when you are using unsigned indices (or you do the AND yourself).

Q: wxTreeCtrl::SelectItem is too slow. What to do? A:

You should definitely freeze the tree while doing it, but 10000 is a too big number of items to select at once in any reasonable scenario. For the trees with such number of items, you would typically delay doing anything with the items until the parent node is expanded (including even adding them to the tree), so the real fix is to only select the items the currently shown items and wait until wxEVT_TREE_ITEM_EXPANDING and only then select all the items under the parent.
